item.research_question: How does the yield and failure strength of a (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high-entropy carbide compare to its base monocarbides (HfC, TaC) during micropillar compression, and which slip systems operate under specific crystallographic orientations at room temperature?
item.material_system: (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high-entropy carbide, HfC monocarbide, TaC monocarbide
item.processing_route: Ball-milling of equiatomic powders followed by spark-plasma sintering (SPS) with a two-step heating profile: 10 min dwell at 1800 °C and 7 min dwell at 2300 °C (Methods section states 2 min at 2300 °C, Abstract/Results state 7 min; text varies slightly but confirms SPS). Micropillars fabricated via FIB with diameter ~2.5 μm and height ~5 μm.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature micro-compression using an Agilent/Keysight G200 nanoindenter with a flat-punch diamond tip (5 μm diameter). Load-controlled mode, max load 100 mN, loading/unloading rate 0.02 mN/s. Grains selected with orientation Φ ~ 14° and φ2 ~ 45°.
key_findings: The (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high-entropy carbide exhibited a yield strength of 6.20 ± 0.12 GPa, which is approximately 60% higher than the hardest base monocarbide HfC (3.93 ± 0.28 GPa).
TaC showed the lowest yield stress at 3.03 ± 0.11 GPa among the tested materials.
The high-entropy carbide demonstrated larger work hardening than HfC and similar ductility to TaC, with total deformation εHEC ~ 0.08 compared to εHfC ~ 0.06 and εTaC ~ 0.1.
Slip analysis confirmed the operation of {110}⟨11¯0⟩ slip systems in all three materials (HfC, TaC, and (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C) at the specific orientation Φ ~ 14° and φ2 ~ 45°.
The calculated critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) for the {110}⟨11¯0⟩ system was 2.79 ± 0.05 GPa for the high-entropy carbide, 1.77 ± 0.13 GPa for HfC, and 1.36 ± 0.05 GPa for TaC.
Cracks initiated on the top surface of micropillars and propagated parallel to {001} facets, attributed to the pile-up of immobile a[001¯] dislocations formed by the interaction of {110} slip bands.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the enhanced strength is due to lattice distortion caused by the difference in atomic size and valence electron concentrations (VEC) of the transition metals, which hinders dislocation motion. The VEC of 8.5 in the high-entropy carbide increases the metallic character compared to HfC (VEC=8), improving ductility. The specific slip system ({110}⟨11¯0⟩) is determined by the crystal orientation and stress conditions (uniaxial compression) where the Schmid factor for {110} exceeds that of {111} for group IV-like behavior, despite TaC typically slipping on {111} under multiaxial indentation.
item.limitations: The lattice structure of the high-entropy carbide has not been completely characterized. The study is confined to uniaxial stress conditions at a specific orientation, which may not represent the behavior under multiaxial stress fields like indentation. The quantitative comparison of micropillar results with theoretical simulations is noted as unreasonable due to differences in dislocation nucleation (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous).
item.future_work: Further DFT simulations are required to test the accuracy of predicting elastic properties for high-entropy carbides. The authors suggest that the dominant slip system during nanoindentation is likely {111}⟨11¯0⟩, differing from the {110} observed in compression, necessitating further investigation into the effect of different stress fields on slip activation.
quotes: It was revealed that (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C had a significantly enhanced yield and failure strength compared to the corresponding base monocarbides
The difference in atomic size and valence electron concentrations (VEC) of the transition metals in the HEC are thought to have a simultaneous lattice distorting effect
This suggests that the nature of the bonding in the high-entropy carbide is similar to TaC, showing a more metallic character than that of HfC
